content: Oxacillin can cause liver toxicity. Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience symptoms of liver damage, such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fever, weakness, unusual fatigue, itching, loss of appetite, light-colored stools, dark-colored urine, or yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice). Individuals who are allergic to oxacillin or any of its ingredients should not use this medication. Your pharmacist can provide a complete list of ingredients in the specific oxacillin product you are prescribed. Oxacillin is typically administered by a healthcare provider in a hospital or clinical setting. If you are storing oxacillin at home, do not share it with others, even if they have the same condition, as it may harm them. Keep oxacillin out of reach of children. Before using oxacillin, inform your healthcare provider about all your health conditions and any medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, or supplements you are taking. This information will help determine if oxacillin is appropriate for you. Specifically, disclose any allergies to penicillin, other medications, corn or corn products, asthma, liver or kidney problems, a history of antibiotic-associated diarrhea, or any other relevant medical conditions. Oxacillin may interact with other medications and supplements. Inform your healthcare provider if you are using any tetracyclines (e.g., doxycycline, minocycline) or probenecid, as these may interact with oxacillin. This may not be a complete list of potential drug interactions. The effects of oxacillin on pregnancy are not well understood. If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, inform your healthcare provider. They will advise you on whether oxacillin is safe to use during pregnancy. Oxacillin passes into breast milk, so let your healthcare provider know if you are breastfeeding or planning to breastfeed. There are no known interactions between oxacillin and food or drinks. However, heavy alcohol consumption can weaken your immune response and make it harder for your body to fight infections. If you or someone else accidentally uses too much oxacillin, seek medical help immediately by calling 911 or contacting a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222. If you miss a dose of oxacillin, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take double or extra doses. Complete the full prescribed course of oxacillin, even if your symptoms improve, to reduce the risk of antibiotic resistance. Oxacillin is an antibiotic used to treat infections caused by certain bacteria. It is not effective against viral infections (e.g., the common cold, influenza, or coronavirus) or non-bacterial infections. Using oxacillin unnecessarily can contribute to antibiotic resistance, making it less effective for future bacterial infections. Oxacillin works by killing bacteria through inhibition of their ability to form cell walls. Oxacillin is available in injectable forms, including 1 g, 2 g, 10 g, 20 mg/mL, and 40 mg/mL preparations. It is administered as an injection into a muscle or blood vessel. Common side effects of oxacillin include pain, swelling, or inflammation at the injection site and rash. Contact your healthcare provider if these side effects bother you. Report any suspected side effects to the FDA at 800-FDA-1088 or Health Canada at 866-234-2345. Serious side effects of oxacillin include severe allergic reactions, seizures, kidney damage, antibiotic-associated diarrhea, blood disorders, and liver damage. Stop using oxacillin and seek immediate medical attention if you experience symptoms such as difficulty breathing, wheezing, rapid heartbeat, fever, swollen lymph nodes, facial swelling, throat tightness, hives, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, stomach cramps, joint pain, or seizures. Kidney damage may present as reduced urination, swelling in the feet or legs, weakness, difficulty breathing, chest pain, confusion, or nausea. Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience these symptoms. Antibiotic-associated diarrhea, caused by an overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile (C. diff), can occur during or up to two months after stopping oxacillin. Symptoms include watery diarrhea, persistent diarrhea, blood in stools, severe stomach cramps, or fever. Contact your healthcare provider if these symptoms occur. Oxacillin can cause blood disorders, such as eosinophilia, agranulocytosis, neutropenia, or bone marrow suppression. Symptoms include fever, shortness of breath, pale or yellowish skin, easy bruising or bleeding, frequent infections, unusual weakness, dizziness, headache, or abnormal heartbeat. Stop using oxacillin and seek medical attention if you experience these symptoms.
